title: Babarvani close
hook: faith that doesn't look away from suffering

segments.voice: Yesterday, truth to power. Your line was speak as it comes. Did one honest thing get said kindly, or did it stay in your mouth? Today the hymns on Babur's invasion come to a close. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-two.

A nurse changing a dressing doesn't look away from the wound. She looks closely and steadily, because looking is part of the care. Turning away would be easier, and it would help no one. Over the last few days this path has read Guru Nanak's hymns on Babur's invasion: the pain named, the women mourned, the truth told to Lalo. Today they close, with one question. What does a faith look like that keeps its eyes open?
screen: `A NURSE LOOKS AT THE WOUND.` → `THE PAIN NAMED, THE WOMEN MOURNED.` → `THE BABARVANI CLOSES.`

segments.voice: Babarvani is the name given to Guru Nanak's hymns about Babur's invasion. Look back over what they do, and three things stand out. First, they look. They don't hurry a massacre into a tidy lesson. They stay with the dust, the broken homes, the ordinary people who paid for a war they never chose. The hymn on ang three hundred sixty even turns to God and asks, in paraphrase: there was so much slaughter, such crying, and did You feel no pain? Second, they keep calling God the Master. The question isn't thrown at an empty sky. The same hymn names the Creator as the Master of all. Protest and trust share a single breath. The cry goes to God because God is still called Master. A question like that is only asked of someone who is there. Third, they're kept. These aren't private notes hidden in a drawer. They sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raga Asa and Raga Tilang, inside the same scripture that sings of joy and praise. A gathering can sing of the Beloved's beauty and, from the same pages, of a town that burned. So the close of the Babarvani gives these days their shape. Faith, in these hymns, isn't a way of looking away. It looks at the worst thing it can see. It names it. It grieves it. It brings the question straight to God, and it keeps saying God's name while it asks. That's today's line: faith that sees.
screen: `FIRST, THEY LOOK: THE PAIN IS NAMED.` · `GOD IS STILL CALLED MASTER.` · `THE HYMNS ARE KEPT IN SCRIPTURE.` · `FAITH THAT ASKS, AND STILL TRUSTS.` · then, large: `FAITH THAT SEES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at one hard truth. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one hard thing you usually glance past. It might be far away, in the news, or close by, on your own street or in your own house. Don't fix it, and don't explain it away. Just look at it for a few breaths, the way the hymns looked at the town. If you pray, you can bring it to God plainly, as a question if it is one. If you don't, simply let it be seen. When your mind tries to change the subject, come back to it once more. The bell holds the time.
Babarvani close. The end of Guru Nanak's hymns on Babur's invasion: they name the suffering, grieve it, and still call God the Master. Today's word.
Your line: faith that sees. Today, when one hard story crosses your screen, stop for one breath and let it count before you scroll on. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: The Babarvani hymns are part of the Guru Granth Sahib and are sung in kirtan and explained in katha, where they are heard as Guru Nanak standing with ordinary people who suffer in war.

original.note: babarvani: the name for Guru Nanak's hymns on Babur's invasion; the word also appears in one of them.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Babarvani is a history lesson about an invasion.
what it means: hymns that look at the suffering, grieve it, and bring the question to God while still calling God Master.
what a scholar hears: the word itself turns up inside a hymn (Asa, ang 417), where some readers take it as Babur's rule or decree spreading over the land.
